n: The second part of Hosea (chapters 4–14) is a series of messages. God brings a legal case against Israel: there is no faithfulness, no loyal love, and no knowledge of God in the land—the three things the covenant required.
The list of sins echoes the Ten Commandments: false swearing, lying, murder, stealing, adultery. Violence follows violence—“blood touches blood.”

f.w: swearing, and lying, and killing, and stealing, and committing adultery

n: Because of human sin, creation itself suffers—the land mourns and even animals, birds, and fish waste away. Sin affects the whole environment.
God says no one should blame others; His real complaint is against the priests. The KJV phrasing is obscure; many translations read, “My contention is with you, O priest.”

f.w: thy people are as they that strive with the priest
f.g: The Hebrew is difficult; it likely means God’s charge is against the priest.

n: Priest and false prophet will stumble day and night, and the nation (their “mother”) will be destroyed.

f.g: The nation of Israel, as in Hosea 2:2.

n: A famous verse: God’s people are destroyed for lack of knowledge. The priests rejected the knowledge of God they were supposed to teach, so God rejects them. Ignorance of God is deadly.

f.w: My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge

n: The more priests there were, the more they sinned. God will turn their glory into disgrace.
The priests profit from the people’s sins—they eat the sin offerings, so they actually want people to keep sinning!

f.w: They eat up the sin of my people
f.g: The priests ate portions of sin offerings, so more sin meant more food for them.

n: “Like people, like priest”—both will be judged for their deeds. Religious office gives no immunity.
They will eat but never be satisfied, and their fertility rites won’t produce offspring—because they stopped heeding the Lord.

f.w: they shall eat, and not have enough

n: Immorality and wine take away understanding. Sin dulls the mind and heart.

f.g: Rob them of understanding or judgment.

n: God’s people ask advice from a piece of wood and seek direction from a stick—forms of pagan divination. A spirit of unfaithfulness has led them astray.

f.g: A divining rod used to seek omens.

n: They offer sacrifices on hilltops under shady trees—popular sites of Canaanite worship. Their daughters and daughters-in-law are drawn into the immorality connected with those rites.

f.w: under oaks and poplars and elms

n: God will not single out the young women for punishment, because the men themselves are worse—consorting with cult prostitutes. A people without understanding will be ruined.

f.g: Cult prostitutes connected with fertility worship.

f.w: the people that doth not understand shall fall

n: A warning to Judah not to follow Israel’s example. Gilgal and Bethel (mockingly called Beth-aven, “house of wickedness”) had become centers of corrupt worship.

f.g: “House of wickedness”—a sarcastic name for Bethel (“house of God”).

n: Israel is as stubborn as a heifer that refuses the yoke. Can the Lord now pasture them like a lamb in an open meadow? (The question implies He cannot.)
Ephraim—another name for the northern kingdom—is joined to idols; “leave him alone.” Persistent sin can bring a point where God lets people go their own way.

f.g: The leading tribe of the north; Hosea uses it for the whole northern kingdom.

n: When their drinking is over, they turn to immorality. Their rulers love shame more than honor.

f.g: Their liquor is gone, or has turned sour; the Hebrew is difficult.

n: A wind will sweep them away in its wings—exile—and they will be ashamed of their sacrifices to false gods.

f.w: The wind hath bound her up in her wings
f.g: A whirlwind will carry them off—a picture of exile.
